extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of mathematics; mathematical problem-solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Heuristics and guidelines for discovering, checking, and presenting mathematical solutions and proofs (e.g., how to decompose/recombine problems, choose starting points, use definitions, and balance intuition and formal proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean method of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Progressing relentlessly from the data to the unknown and from the hypothesis to the conclusion (the 'Euclidean' order of synthesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excellent for checking the argument in detail (each particular point), but poor for conveying the main line of the argument to a reader who never heard of it before. It often proceeds in the opposite order to the natural order of invention. Recommended that students examine their own arguments in the Euclidean manner to check steps, but teachers should not present many proofs purely in this manner. Prefer presenting an intuitive sketch of the main idea first and the Euclidean details afterwards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check every step (including the last assertion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify each individual step of an argument; if each step is correct, the whole argument is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When checking, rely on intuition or formal rules as appropriate. Try to check both intuitively and formally when possible. Emphasize checking the final assertion as well as intermediate steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance intuition and formal proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to see the result intuitively and to provide a formal proof; intuition and formal manipulation may lead or follow one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuitive insight may rush ahead of formal proof (and vice versa). It is a useful exercise to both see a step clearly and to be able to prove it formally. In classroom time may be limited, but striving for both strengthens understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify principal parts: unknown, data, condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin problem analysis by asking: What is the unknown? What are the data? What is the condition?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the problem as a whole first helps judge which details are essential. Often reasonable to start detailed examination by considering the unknown, the data, and the condition separately; further decompose parts of the condition or data as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer starting from the unknown (working backwards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Try starting reasoning from the unknown (look at the unknown) to recollect or invent similar problems; this often yields a better approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting from the data is also sometimes successful and must be tried. The text recommends trying the unknown-first approach but explicitly illustrates that both directions deserve illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive something useful from the data (introduce auxiliaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask 'Could you derive something useful from the data?' and introduce auxiliary elements (lines, points, constructions) suggested by the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures and auxiliary constructions often connect the data to the unknown; when a figure is 'too empty' add useful auxiliary lines. The best way to progress when stuck is often to ask this question and try simple, natural auxiliary constructions first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose and recombine gradually
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose the problem into parts and recombine elements to form new, more accessible problems or auxiliary problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the whole before going into detail; avoid going into unnecessary or premature detail. Decompose gradually and only as far as needed; recombination may produce auxiliary problems that are easier to solve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three recombination strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: When transforming the proposed problem by recombination, one may (1) keep the unknown and change the rest (data/condition), (2) keep the data and change the rest (unknown/condition), or (3) change both unknown and data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer to keep the unknown and change as little as feasible; a good method is omitting some parts of the condition without adding new clauses. If changing both, be wary of drifting too far from the original problem; interchanging unknown with a datum is an interesting variant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weaken condition to obtain loci and intersect them
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep only a part of the condition to find the locus of points satisfying that part; the desired object can often be obtained as intersection of two such loci.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a common pattern in geometric constructions: reduce to constructing a point, describe loci for partial conditions, and take their intersection. The method generalizes to characterizing sets of objects satisfying part of a condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: For 'problems to prove': analyze hypothesis and conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: In problems of proof, the principal parts are the hypothesis and the conclusion; understand them thoroughly and decompose the hypothesis if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After decomposing, try recombining into another theorem by (1) keeping the conclusion and changing the hypothesis (seek familiar theorems with same conclusion), (2) keeping the hypothesis and changing the conclusion (derive useful consequences), or (3) changing both hypothesis and conclusion if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go back to definitions (eliminate technical terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: When unfamiliar or inflated technical terms appear, replace them by their defining facts: introduce new elements implied by the definition and use those relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminating technical terms by using their definitions often clarifies the problem (introduce lines/points specified by the definition). This operation is important both for devising and for checking arguments; if a solution never uses the definition or theorems about a notion, the solution is suspect. Pascal's rule: mentally substitute definitions for the defined terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate definition when multiple exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Many derived notions have more than one definition; choose the definition that best fits the case and suggests useful methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a sphere can be defined as a locus or as a surface of revolution; the choice affects available approximation and solution techniques (Archimedes chose the revolving-circle view to approximate the sphere's surface).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use known theorems when available; otherwise use definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to apply theorems about a derived notion or to work from its definition depending on what you know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you know many theorems about the notion, look for a suitable theorem; if you know only the definition, you must use the definition. The choice depends on your acquaintance with the object's properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check use of essential notions in arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating a proposed solution, ensure the solver has taken into account and used essential notions, definitions, or known theorems relevant to the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a presenter never says something substantial about a key derived notion (definition or theorem), their solution is not convincing. Inspect how the notion is used and whether essential facts have been applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive detail; prioritize essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Too many or too minute particulars may obscure the main point; do not lose sight of the whole by diving prematurely into details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the problem as a whole first to judge which details will ultimately be necessary. Teachers cannot expect all students to avoid starting with details, but one should reserve effort for the essential and decompose gradually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance and emotional factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination, hope, and persistence play an important role in solving serious problems; intellectual effort alone may not suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willpower to endure years of toil and disappointment is often required for serious scientific problems. Expect determination to fluctuate with progress, and cultivate perseverance.
